evidence.title: Role-Prompting in Frontier Large Language Models Influences Clinical Reasoning in Complex Medical Cases
evidence.outcome: primary ethical value shift under insurer role
evidence.effect: Shifted primary ethical values from beneficence (27%) to financial stewardship (20%) across all LLMs
evidence.quote: The insurer role shifted primary ethical values from beneficence (27%) to financial stewardship (20%) across all LLMs.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (25 cases x 3 roles x 3 runs x 3 models)

evidence.title: Disparities in AI-Based Prior Authorization for Head and Neck Reconstruction: A Large Language Model Analysis
evidence.venue: World journal of otorhinolaryngology - head and neck surgery
evidence.outcome: Bias in LLM-simulated insurance coverage decisions with limited clinical information
evidence.effect: LLM prior authorization outputs showed significant demographic disparities; adding tumor-specific information markedly skewed recommendations towards RFFF across sociodemographic backgrounds.
evidence.quote: On sensitivity analysis, inclusion of tumor-specific information markedly skewed recommendations towards RFFF across sociodemographic backgrounds.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether restricting automated coverage systems to administrative tasks, with determinations based on individual need and current guidelines, changes denial rates or patient outcomes. Two simulation studies suggest that large language models placed in insurer roles may shift toward financial priorities and produce demographic disparities, which documents the hazard but does not evaluate this safeguard.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Both available studies are level 4 vignette simulations run offline with large language models. They show that the hazard can appear in simulated settings. They measure model outputs rather than actual coverage determinations, denials, or patient outcomes under any restriction policy.

Across 675 responses from three models, the insurer role shifted primary ethical values from beneficence (27%) to financial stewardship (20%). This suggests automated systems may weigh cost over clinical need when framed as payers. No study examined whether limiting these systems to administrative work, or requiring physician review before denial, stops such errors before they reach patients.

Across 19,900 simulated prior authorization decisions, model outputs showed significant demographic disparities. Adding tumor-specific information skewed recommendations toward RFFF across sociodemographic backgrounds. The study did not report Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency subgroups, and no study tested whether individual-need determinations reduce these disparities.

The single endorsement is guidance stating that treating physicians must have the opportunity to discuss medical necessity with the reviewing physician before an adverse determination. This guidance addresses one element of the recommendation, physician-to-physician review. No study cited here supports it.

Under the endorsed requirement, a physician would discuss medical necessity before care is denied, so the decision would not rest on an automated system alone. The simulation findings suggest why patients may distrust algorithmic denials. No study measured whether this safeguard preserves access, shortens delays, or improves trust.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare coverage determinations, overturned denials, time to care, and patient outcomes between payers that limit automated systems to administrative functions with physician review and payers that allow automated determinations. These studies should use real claims data and report results by payer type, language, literacy, and demographic group.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither hazard study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tested the practice. The demographic disparities seen in simulated prior authorization suggest these groups may face added risk. Whether the recommendation protects them remains unknown.
